title: Comisionado Residente exige a la AAA datos de agua perdida para atender problema
text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — El Comisionado Residente de Puerto Rico, Pablo José Hernández, busca obtener de la Autoridad de Acueductos y Alcantarillados (AAA) los datos necesarios para identificar donde se están perdiendo los recursos, qué proyectos necesitan atención y dónde puede intervenir el gobierno federal para acelerar soluciones a la crisis de agua.

En una carta al presidente ejecutivo de la AAA, Luis R. González Delgado, el Comisionado Residente solicitó datos e información sobre las pérdidas de agua – estimadas en cerca del 60% del agua que produce la AAA, los retrasos en proyectos críticos y el uso de fondos federales disponibles para mejorar el sistema.

“A pesar de que la AAA conoce de este problema por años, todavía no pueda medir con precisión cuánta agua se pierde.” escribió el Comisionado Residente. “Desde el Congreso, quisiéramos ayudar a resolver este problema de pérdida de agua. Para ello, necesitamos conocer la magnitud del problema y qué necesitan para resolverlo.”

Uno de los principales retos es la cantidad de agua que nunca llega a los hogares. Informes recientes estiman que la AAA pierde cerca del 60% del agua que produce. El Comisionado Residente busca identificar dónde se necesita mayor atención y qué acciones pueden impulsarse desde Washington. El solicitó detalles sobre:

Dónde se pierde el agua y qué áreas requieren atención inmediata.

Qué fondos federales están disponibles y cómo se están utilizando.

Qué proyectos están atrasados y qué impide que avancen.

Qué mejoras hacen falta para reducir las pérdidas de agua.

Qué apoyo adicional necesita la AAA de Washington para mejorar el sistema.

El Comisionado Residente también solicitó información sobre cómo se utilizan los fondos de FEMA y del Programa de Subvención en Bloque para el Desarrollo Comunitario para la Recuperación ante Desastres (CDBG-DR) para atender las pérdidas y aumentar la capacidad de los embalses, con el fin de identificar cuáles áreas necesitan atención inmediata.

“Nos preocupa el uso apropiado de fondos federales. Tenemos información que establece que había fondos suficientes para múltiples proyectos desde el 2021, pero, que sepamos, sólo han sido utilizados en la primera fase del dragado de Carraízo; sobraron fondos y no es hasta ahora que se habla de otros 18 proyectos de dragado —un poco tarde si nos dejamos llevar por la crisis actual de agua.” concluyó el Comisionado Residente.

Esta gestión forma parte de los esfuerzos que el Comisionado Residente ha liderado para atender la crisis de agua, movilizar recursos federales y acelerar soluciones. Es la tercera comunicación que dirige a la AAA para dar seguimiento a estos esfuerzos e identificar cómo el gobierno federal puede ayudar.

title: RELEASE: REP. HILL AWARDS GOLDEN FLEECE TO FAA AND TSA FOR GAPS IN CYBERSECURITY
text:
Rep. French Hill (AR-02) today announced that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) are the latest recipients of his Golden Fleece Award for recently identified shortcomings in their oversight of aviation cybersecurity risks.According to GAO, nearly 44,000 flights carrying 3 million passengers fly the skies of the United States every day. As aviation systems become increasingly connected, protecting avionics and ground systems from cyber threats is essential to maintaining the safety and reliability of America’s aerospace.

Rep. Hill said, "Air travel is an essential part of American life and critical to the economic health of our nation. It's imperative that passengers, as well as pilots and flight attendants, have confidence that we’re doing everything in our power to make sure they take off and land safely. Guarding the cyber systems that keep our nation's aviation infrastructure protected is a major part of that effort. While the FAA and TSA have taken steps to address cybersecurity challenges, gaps remain that require continued attention. Federal agencies responsible for keeping our planes flying must ensure they have defined responsibilities and effective risk management practices in place."

In his letter to Federal Aviation Administration Chief Information Security Officer Gina Fisk, Rep. Hill writes:

Dear Director Fisk,

I write to inform you that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) are the latest recipients of my Golden Fleece Award for shortcomings in their cybersecurity strategies. Nearly 44,000 flights and 3 million passengers travel through the National Airspace System (NAS) each day, underscoring the need for robust cybersecurity as avionics and ground systems become increasingly interconnected.

Between 2020 and 2025, the aerospace sector reported nearly 2,000 cybersecurity incidents to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). These incidents highlighted vulnerabilities such as inadequate software patching, internet-accessible operational technology, outdated software, vulnerable remote services that could enable unauthorized access to avionics, and ground systems or manipulation of critical information.

The Departments of Transportation (DOT) and Homeland Security (DHS) share responsibility for overseeing cybersecurity risk across America's transportation sector. Their authorities are established through federal statutes, including Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA), the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, and the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024. The National Institute of Standards and Technology's (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 further provides guidance for managing cybersecurity risk and transitioning to a Zero Trust architecture.

While the FAA's cybersecurity strategy clearly defines agency roles and responsibilities, comparable TSA planning documents do not. For example, the TSA Strategy for 2018–2026 does not explicitly establish cybersecurity-specific goals or objectives to support aviation security. Moreover, it is no longer fully aligned with DHS's broader cybersecurity strategy. Other planning documents, including Administrator's Intent 3.0 and the 2018 TSA Cybersecurity Roadmap, similarly lack clear objectives and fail to define TSA's roles and responsibilities for overseeing airport and aircraft cybersecurity programs.

These documents also do not clearly identify the offices responsible for implementing their stated goals and objectives. Although Administrator's Intent 3.0 directed TSA to update its cybersecurity roadmap between 2018 and 2026, the agency has yet to do so.

The absence of clearly defined cybersecurity roles has contributed to confusion among manufacturers, airlines, and other aviation stakeholders regarding TSA's cybersecurity responsibilities. Although FAA has defined its role, greater interagency clarity would strengthen coordination across the aviation sector.

The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) requires agencies to report cybersecurity expenditures through the Cyber Budget Data Request process to inform the President's budget. However, FAA did not report complete information on its Information Security/Cybersecurity Program because it was not required to report all cybersecurity spending. Consequently, the Administration and Congress could lack a complete understanding of the agency's cybersecurity investments, including research and development activities.

While the FAA's Cybersecurity Strategy aligns with several federal Zero Trust practices, it does not fully align with NIST's Zero Trust Architecture guidance. The strategy fully aligns with only three of seven identified practices, and partially addresses the remaining four. Full implementation is necessary to effectively manage cybersecurity risks.

I appreciate the FAA's efforts to implement federal and industry best practices to mitigate cybersecurity vulnerabilities affecting avionics and ground systems. The FAA must continue implementing its cybersecurity posture to ensure the safety, security, and resilience of the National Airspace System.

If additional statutory authority is necessary to address these concerns, I encourage you to notify me promptly. I also welcome any technical assistance the FAA can provide to assist Congress in addressing these issues. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

title: Maryland Delegation Members’ Statement on State’s Victory in Lawsuit to Restore Greenbelt FBI Headquarters
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) and Members of Maryland’s Congressional delegation, including U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks (both D-MD) and U.S. Representatives Glenn Ivey (MD-04), Kweisi Mfume (MD-07), Jamie Raskin (MD-08), Sarah Elfreth (MD-03), and Johnny Olszewski (MD-02), released the following statement regarding the State of Maryland’s victory in its lawsuit to restore the FBI headquarters project to Greenbelt, Maryland:

“For years, Team Maryland has fought to bring the men and women of the FBI a headquarters that meets their mission and their needs. After a years-long, competitive, and transparent process, Greenbelt, Maryland, was selected as the site for that new headquarters, based on its merits – including its ability to provide a secure space for the Bureau while ensuring the cost-effective use of taxpayer dollars. The Trump Administration had no grounds to ignore this selection, or redirect even one penny that Congress specifically appropriated for construction of the competitively selected site. We’re glad to see the Court acknowledge this fact, ruling that the Trump Administration’s actions are unlawful and void. This is an important step forward for the rule of law. This process began in 2009, and it’s past time it was concluded. Hopefully, the Trump Administration will agree with the conclusion that the Congress, the General Services Administration, and the District Court have all found, which is that Greenbelt is the proper home of the FBI. We will not stop fighting to fulfill our promise to the men and women of the Bureau to deliver a new, secure headquarters in Maryland so they can do their work without compromising their safety or our national security.”

title: 54 House Democrats Raise Concerns Over Trump Administration’s Critical Minerals Agreements
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), Ways and Means Trade Subcommittee Ranking Member Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.), and Congressman Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.) led 51 of their House Democratic colleagues in calling on the Trump administration to address concerns about its recently announced critical minerals agreements.

The deals lack transparency and enforceable protections for labor rights, human rights and the environment, while potentially enriching Trump administration insiders and placing financial risk onto American taxpayers without congressional oversight.

The New York Times has even reported that companies linked to the families of President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick would profit from a U.S.-backed critical minerals agreement in Kazakhstan.

“In light of these concerns, we call for a transparent and accountable negotiation process, alongside a clear commitment to advancing high-road, sustainable critical minerals mining and processing,” the members wrote. “The United States must also engage partner countries with respect for their sovereignty and support value-addition in critical minerals supply chains that strengthens emerging economies and ensures exploitative practices of the past are not repeated.”

In addition to Huffman, Sánchez, and Jackson, the letter was signed by Gabe Amo (D-R.I.), Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), Becca Balint (D-Vt.), Donald Beyer (D-Va.), Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.), Julia Brownley (D-Calif.), Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.), Greg Casar (D-Texas), Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), Joaquin Castro (D-Texas), Judy Chu (D-Calif.), Danny Davis (D-Ill.), Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.), Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.), Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), Sarah Elfreth (D-Md.), Dwight Evans (D-Pa.), John Garamendi (D-Calif.), Jesús García (D-Ill.), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.), Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.), Pablo Hernández (D-Puerto Rico), Hank Johnson (D-Ga.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), John Larson (D-Conn.), Summer Lee (D-Pa.), Mike Levin (D-Calif.), Betty McCollum (D-Minn.), James McGovern (D-Mass.), Kelly Morrison (D-Minn.), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Johnny Olszewski (D-Md.), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), Nellie Pou (D-N.J.), Mike Quigley (D-Ill.), Luz Rivas (D-Calif.), Deborah Ross (D-N.C.), Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.), Janice Schakowsky (D-Ill.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.), Dina Titus (D-Nev.), Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.) and Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-N.J.).

Full text of the letter is available HERE and follows:

August 17, 2026

Ambassador Greer

U.S. Trade Representative

600 17th St. NW,

Washington, D.C. 20508

Secretary Rubio

U.S. Department of State

2201 C Street NW

Washington, D.C. 20520

Secretary Lutnick

U.S. Department of Commerce

1401 Constitution Ave., NW

Washington, D.C. 20230

Secretary Bessent

U.S. Department of the Treasury

1500 Pennsylvania Ave., NW

Washington, D.C. 20220

Dear Ambassador Greer, Secretary Rubio, Secretary Lutnick, and Secretary Bessent:

We write to raise serious concerns with the administration’s recent international agreements related to critical minerals, including framework agreements, agreements on reciprocal trade, action plans, memoranda of understanding (MOU), and a potential Plurilateral Agreement on Trade in Critical Minerals. While we have long supported efforts to strengthen U.S. critical minerals supply chains to build our clean energy and technology industries and to reduce reliance on China, several of these “deals” raise concerns regarding transparency, labor and human rights, environmental protections, and insufficient congressional oversight.

As you know, poorly regulated mining and minerals processing has a well-documented record of environmental damage, displacement and harm to Indigenous communities, and widespread labor and human rights violations. Any agreement facilitating trade in critical minerals must directly address these harms and avoid reinforcing extractive models that prioritize mining profits over communities and workers.

All minerals-related trade negotiations must also allow for broad public participation and congressional review and approval, as required by Article 1, Section 8 of the Constitution. We were alarmed to hear about the administration’s threats to use “trade-restricting measures” in negotiating critical minerals agreements which directly usurp Congressional prerogatives on trade.

Our scrutiny of executive overreach in critical minerals agreements is not new. Republican and Democratic congressional leaders alike sharply criticized the Biden administration’s critical minerals trade deal with Japan for circumventing Congress’s trade authority and lacking enforceable labor, human rights, and environmental standards.

Unfortunately, the Trump administration expanded this approach, announcing critical minerals deals and related provisions in the broader “reciprocal” trade deals without meaningful consultation with Congress nor the communities that would be most impacted. A letter sent to Secretary Rubio by more than 50 House members last August requesting basic information about the negotiations of a critical minerals deal with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) went unanswered.

We were alarmed to learn the Trump administration has since signed a “Strategic Partnership Agreement” (SPA) with the DRC which calls for sweeping changes to the DRC’s constitution and grants U.S. companies a “right of first offer” on mining concessions. The SPA has paved the way for foreign mining companies to extract the DRC’s mineral wealth amid a violent conflict, all while mass violence and human rights violations continue. In this context, reports the U.S. helped fund a paramilitary force to guard mining operations in the DRC and may lift Magnitsky Act sanctions on businessman Dan Gertler to facilitate a cobalt deal, are especially troubling.

We were further troubled to learn that U.S. development assistance is being used as leverage in critical minerals negotiations. It is callous and unacceptable that the State Department threatened to withhold HIV medicines and other lifesaving assistance for the Zambian people to pressure the Zambian government into signing a critical minerals agreement with the U.S. The Trump administration’s cuts to foreign aid, particularly for healthcare assistance, have also threatened workforce stability, economic development, and broader U.S. strategic interests in partner countries.

We also note significant issues with the critical minerals provisions included in several Agreements on Reciprocal Trade (ART). The ART with Malaysia prevents export restrictions on critical minerals which some emerging economies rely on to promote value addition, increase government revenue, and support downstream development. ARTs with Argentina, Ecuador, Cambodia and Bangladesh explicitly require countries to facilitate U.S. mining investment in their countries without requiring any binding environmental, labor, or human rights commitments.

In addition, provisions within the MOU concluded with Malaysia establish an institutional channel for the United States to influence mining policy and governance in Malaysia while skirting Congressional involvement, international agreements, and public debate. The text explicitly encourages “streamlining permitting processes”. Under the Trump administration “streamlining” policies for domestic mining has included dramatically limiting environmental review, eliminating opportunities for public input, and weakening or repealing environmental protections. This MOU, and others modeled on it, could therefore provide a channel for the Trump administration to push its deregulatory agenda onto partner countries without scrutiny.

Finally, we are deeply concerned these deals commit U.S. taxpayers to billions in direct loans and loan guarantees by the Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and Export-Import Bank and other federal equity investments in mining and processing. These structures shift risk onto U.S. taxpayers while encouraging companies to take on riskier projects. If projects succeed, companies keep the profits; if they fail, taxpayers help absorb losses.

Absent strong transparency and accountability measures, these investments and loan guarantees raise risks of conflicts of interest, self-dealing, preferential treatment, and weakened oversight. The Export-Import Bank inspector general position has remained vacant for months, and the recent DFC reauthorization expanded the agency’s authorities while reducing congressional oversight, leaving hundreds of billions of dollars in U.S. government-backed financing without credible safeguards against corruption or misuse of taxpayer funds. Recent reporting by the New York Times that members of the Trump and Lutnick families could be enriched through U.S.-financed critical minerals deals underscores this concern.

These risks are compounded by the Trump administration’s pursuit of critical minerals agreements that include price floors. Depending on the goals and design of coordinated price support mechanisms, they could facilitate cartel-like behavior inconsistent with U.S. antitrust law and inadvertently benefit Chinese firms elsewhere in the critical minerals supply chain. Without rigorous safeguards, traceability requirements, and restrictions on participation by Chinese state-linked firms, these mechanisms could inadvertently reinforce China’s dominance in global supply chains rather than reduce U.S. dependence on it.

In light of these concerns, we call for a transparent and accountable negotiation process, alongside a clear commitment to advancing high-road, sustainable critical minerals mining and processing. The United States must also engage partner countries with respect for their sovereignty and support value-addition in critical minerals supply chains that strengthens emerging economies and ensures exploitative practices of the past are not repeated.

title: Smith Visits Naeger Forest Products in Ste. Genevieve County
text:
STE. GENEVIEVE COUNTY, Mo. – Congressman Jason Smith (MO-08) visited Naeger Forest Products in Ste. Genevieve County recently, touring the sawmill with owner Mike Naeger to discuss the challenges facing Missouri’s timber industry.

Congressman Smith said, “Mike has spent more than four decades building this sawmill into one that produces some of the highest-quality cedar in the country, and it was clear from our conversation just how much pride he takes in that work. We talked about the flood of cheap, fake wood products coming in from China, the toll the railroad merger has taken on the tie market, and the need to open up new domestic and foreign markets for Missouri timber. Our forest products industry is every bit as important to America’s supply chain security as our farm, food, and pharmaceutical industries, and I’ll keep fighting in Washington to make sure it’s treated that way.”

Mike Naeger has worked in logging for 41 years and opened his sawmill 34 years ago. The mill specializes in cutting Aromatic and Eastern Red Cedar sourced from within a 100-mile radius of Perry, St. Francois, and Jefferson Counties. The mill also processes hardwood, selling oak to McLain Forest Products in Van Buren and pine to buyers in Indiana and Illinois, moving roughly 3 million board feet of lumber a year.

Congressman Smith also discussed the challenges facing Missouri’s timber industry with Missouri Forest Products Association President Brian Brookshire, including the decline of the industry in recent years, competition from imported imitation wood products from China, and the impact of railroad consolidation on the tie and barrel whiskey markets. They also discussed efforts to have the U.S. Forest Service and Department of Commerce work to expand markets for American-made wood products.

The Fix Our Forests Act, which Congressman Smith voted for, allows for more active management of fire-prone federal forestland through logging, thinning, and restoration projects that reduce wildfire risk and improve forest health. He continues to push for policies that support domestic timber production, expand markets for American wood products, and reduce reliance on foreign imports.

title: Jayapal Demands Answers on So-Called “Donroe” Doctrine Policies that Risk Destabilizing the Western Hemisphere
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), a Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, is calling on Secretary of State Marco Rubio to answer for the regional implications of the “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, and ground U.S. foreign policy toward the Western Hemisphere on the principles of mutual respect and advancement of human rights.

“As Members of Congress, we are asked to accept that this doctrine now governs U.S. policy toward every nation in the Western Hemisphere — yet we still lack the basic information needed to understand what it means in practice, what authorities it assumes, and what human costs this new posture has already claimed in communities across the Americas,” wrote the Members. “Taken together, the interventions conducted under the banner of the ‘Donroe’ Doctrine appear to follow a partisan playbook: the endorsement of favored candidates, the placement of political allies, the weaponization of tariffs and sanctions, and, where those fail, the application of direct military force. These are tactics that destabilize our hemisphere and endanger our neighbors”

The “Donroe” Doctrine appears to have three main facets:

Lethal force without Congressional authorization or due process: Since September 2025, the U.S. military has carried out over five dozen lethal boat strikes, killing well over 200 people with no due process.

Economic coercion as a form of collective punishment: In January, the President imposed what amounts to a full blockade on fuel shipments to the island. Elsewhere, sanctions and tariffs have been used to shield a political ally from prosecution and to pressure an electorate before it votes.

Interference in the democratic life of sovereign nations: Across the hemisphere, the administration has openly intervened in sovereign electoral processes, including in Honduras and Colombia.

Jayapal is leading a Congressional Delegation to the Panamerican Congress, where hemispheric partners will discuss alternative visions for security and prosperity in the Western Hemisphere rooted in respect for the sovereignty of countries across the region, international law, and the needs of poor and working-class communities.

The letter was also signed by Representatives Greg Casar (TX-35), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Jesús G. “Chuy” García (IL-04), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Summer Lee (PA-12), Ilhan Omar (MN-05), Delia C. Ramirez (IL-03), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Nydia Velázquez (NY-07), and Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT).

title: WCVB: Democrats hold ‘shadow hearing’ on deadly ICE shooting in Maine
text:
BIDDEFORD, Maine — Massachusetts Rep. Katherine Clark and other high-ranking Democrats held a hearing in Maine on Monday about the killing of a man by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement

officer last month, raising questions about the agency’s actions and the information it used during the operation.

Federal investigators said ICE officers opened fire when Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, a Colombian husband and father, drove his car toward an officer.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said agents were conducting surveillance when a car left the residence. DHS said the driver failed to stop, and an officer opened fire, fearing for public safety. The officers involved were not wearing body cameras.

Guerrero’s parents, Dora Guerrero and Omar Durán Plata, received a standing ovation during the hearing.

Speaking through a translator, they said, “I ask only of God and the justice system that my son’s case be brought to light.”

The family’s lawyer, Ben Gideon, questioned the legality of the traffic stop.

“There was no lawful justification for stopping the car in the first place,” Gideon said.

New details about ICE’s intended target were revealed during the hearing. Maine Rep. Chellie Pingree said, “We have learned that ICE’s intended target, Johan Sebastian’s roommate and the owner of the car he was driving that morning, also did not have a final removal order.”

In July, ICE stated it was targeting someone with a “final order of removal” and claimed, “The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and fearing for public safety an officer discharged his weapon.”

“We know that Johan Sebastian was not the target of the operation. He did not have a final order of removal. He had a pending asylum case and a valid work permit,” Pingree added.

In the so-called shadow hearing, an unofficial proceeding, representatives heard from Maine’s governor, Biddeford’s mayor, the Guerrero family’s attorney, and immigrant rights advocates. Clark, the Democratic House Whip, was joined by Pingree and Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, ranking member of the Committee on Homeland Security.

“This is a mass secret police force that has terrorized children, trampled on our Constitution and wielded violence as a political weapon,” Clark said.

“If ICE cannot be reigned in and fundamentally reformed, then it is time to abolish it.” Her remarks were met with cheers,” Mills said.

Monday’s hearing was held in Biddeford, where Guerrero was killed.

Guerrero’s death was the fourth deadly shooting linked to the federal immigration crackdown this year:

Renee Good, 37, was shot and killed by federal agents in Minneapolis on Jan. 7. Agents stopped her sport utility vehicle during demonstrations and opened fire after video showed her pull forward.

Just a few weeks later, federal agents shot and killed VA nurse Alex Pretti, 37, in Minneapolis during a protest. Part of that confrontation was also caught on video.

On July 7, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, was shot and killed after allegedly trying to evade ICE agents in Houston. The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Araujo, a Mexican national, ignored commands and attempted to ram an agent who fired his weapon in self-defense.

No one has been charged in connection with any of the deaths.

—

title: Whip Clark: “ICE Is a Danger to Every Person in Every Community”
text:
BIDDEFORD, ME — Today, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark (MA-5) joined Ranking Member Bennie Thompson (MS-2), Rep. Chellie Pingree (ME-1), and Rep. Troy Carter (LA-2) for a field hearing on the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by ICE. Below is a transcript of her remarks:

“Thank you to Ranking Member Bennie Thompson for convening this important hearing. And a huge thanks to Congresswoman Pingree for being our host, for being an advocate, and for continuing to seek justice and the truth. We are so very grateful to you. I also want to thank my colleague, Congressman Troy Carter from New Orleans, Louisiana. And Governor Mills, thank you for being with us. But my most deep gratitude for our witnesses, especially Mr. Durán Guerrero’s family. We so appreciate you being here in this time of grief, and pain, and loss. And we appreciate all of you, the community members of Biddeford and those who traveled here to make sure that we continue to shine a light on what happened here.

“This pain is being felt across the country.

“Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was a husband and a father who wanted to give his 3-year-old girl a shot at the American Dream. His cold-blooded murder at the hands of a dangerous, out-of-control ICE agent — at the hands of an abuser with a history of violence against his own family — it’s not only a tragedy for this community, it’s a despicable moral stain on our country as a whole.

“This isn’t someone ICE was looking for. This isn’t a warrant they were executing. This wasn’t a suspect. He hadn’t done anything illegal. This was a random traffic stop that quickly escalated into outright murder. All with ICE’s bodycams off. Even ICE knew that this had gone horribly wrong. Even they decided to halt all vehicular stops in the aftermath, until Trump reversed that decision… 24 hours later.

“If this can happen to Johan, it can happen to anyone. If this can happen in Biddeford, Maine, this can happen anywhere. ICE is a danger to every person in every community in which they are active if they are not held accountable. We are witnessing systematic, state-sanctioned terror inflicted on innocent people by their own government.

“And we condemn it. House Democrats condemn it. All of us across this country condemn it, except for a specific group.

“Republicans in the House and in Congress continue to fund, greenlight, and cover up for this reckless agency.

“So our job here today, together, is to shine a light on the truth. And the truth is these are not protectors of our communities, of our laws, of our borders. This is a masked, secret police force that has terrorized children, trampled on our Constitution, and wielded violence as a political weapon.

“And the truth is the American people have had enough. Enough fear. Enough terror. Enough inaction from Republicans that won’t stand up to this injustice.

“So, we thank you again for being here today. I thank the witnesses, not only for being here today but the work you do across Maine every single day for immigrant communities. And I thank you for speaking out and for sharing your stories. I’m grateful to my colleagues and to the family of Johan Sebastián for this important and urgent discussion. I yield back.”

title: Lawmakers Raise Concerns Around Social Media Deepfakes, Meta’s Rollback of Election Safeguards
text:
Washington, D.C. – As artificial intelligence makes it increasingly easy to spread deepfakes and other deceptive political content, federal lawmakers are raising concerns that Meta’s rollback of election integrity safeguards could leave voters more vulnerable to misinformation and disinformation ahead of the 2026 elections.

Congressman Kevin Mullin (CA-15) is leading a coalition of 18 lawmakers in calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to provide more transparency in how the company will protect users from AI-generated disinformation and election interference after the social media giant discontinued its third-party fact-checking program and other key tools to stop the spread of false and deceptive election information.

“Generative AI has made it easier than ever to create convincing deepfakes and other deceptive content, and we’re already seeing these tactics used to influence America’s elections,” Rep. Mullin said. “Meta, headquartered in my district, has rolled back key safeguards over the last few years designed to prevent the spread of misinformation, and this raises serious questions about whether it is prepared to meet today’s rapidly evolving threats. While Meta is just one company, it runs some of the largest social media platforms in the world: Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp. Its decisions have a major impact on what Americans see every single day. American voters have a right to know whether what they are seeing online about candidates and elections is real or fake.”

Over 53% of U.S. adults report getting news from social media platforms, making the integrity of information shared online increasingly critical to a healthy democracy. The rapid expansion of generative AI has introduced new challenges by allowing bad actors to create realistic deepfakes, cloned voices, and synthetic personas that can be used to impersonate candidates, spread false information, and manipulate voters at scale.

Deepfake content has already been deployed in primary elections across the country with AI-generated campaign ads impersonating political candidates and their opinions. At the same time, fake influencer accounts and profiles, advocating for certain views and candidates are amassing millions of views. For example, in April 2026, it was reported that a 22-year-old medical student in India used AI tools to fabricate “Emily Hart,” a fake conservative MAGA “influencer,” collecting thousands of subscribers before Instagram finally removed it for fraudulent activity. As AI tools make it easier to create convincing but false online identities, images, and videos, social media platforms must have effective safeguards in place to prevent deceptive content from reaching and influencing millions of users. Instead, in just the last month Meta launched a new AI tool to create deepfakes based on users’ likeness without their consent, and the feature had to be removed shortly after it was launched.

“We are writing to express our concern over Meta’s rollback of key safeguards designed to prevent the spread of misinformation on its platforms, and the risk this could pose to the 2026 elections in the United States,” the lawmakers wrote. “We believe that Meta’s approach to the 2026 election cycle is inadequate to address the threats now facing American elections – particularly given Meta’s rollback of fact-checking, the automation of risk review, and the proliferation of AI generated content on Meta’s platforms.”

In the letter authored by Rep. Mullin, the lawmakers highlight concerns regarding Meta’s discontinuation of its third-party fact-checking program, which helped to remove or down rank fraudulent or harmful content, and its move to rely on users who choose to write “Community Notes” instead. The letter also raises concerns about reports that Meta has shifted more privacy and integrity reviews to AI systems with less human oversight, and whether the platforms require social media influencers to disclose when they are paid to promote a political candidate.

Specifically, the lawmakers ask for Meta to share:

How does Meta’s staffing and budget for election integrity differ in 2026 compared to 2020 and 2024?

What policies and enforcement mechanisms does Meta have for non-advertising AI-generated political content, such as deepfake videos, synthetic audio, and impersonation accounts? On average, how long does it take to remove this content across platforms?

Does Meta require social media influencers who are paid to post political content to disclose that they are being paid and who is funding the content?

Does Meta require advertisers to disclose when AI-generated images or audio are used in political ads in ways that could mislead users?

Do state and local election officials have a dedicated way to report misleading voting information to Meta? If so, how is that reporting system staffed, and what was the average response time for reports from election officials in 2025 and 2026 to date?

How does Meta enforce Facebook’s real-name policy, and what verification is required? What steps does Meta take to prevent fake or bot accounts on Instagram and Threads?

What information must non-paid Facebook Pages and third-party-managed accounts on Meta platforms disclose about who controls the account? Does Meta verify that information, and if so, how?

What impact has Meta’s Community Notes program had since January 2025 and how does it compare to the amount of misinformation flagged through Meta’s former fact-checking program?

How much content has Meta removed for violating its Community Standards since January 2025, compared with 2024 and 2023?

In addition to Rep. Mullin, the letter was signed by Reps. Ansari (AZ-03), Beyer (VA-08), Casar (TX-35), Dean (PA-04), Dingell (MI-04), Foushee (NC-04), Garcia (TX-29), Goldman (NY-10), Grijalva (AZ-07), Magaziner (RI-02), Morelle(NY-25), Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14), Pelosi (CA-11), Sewell (AL-07), Simon (CA-12), Smith (WA-09), Thanedar (MI-13), Williams (GA-05).

title: $200,000 Grant to Expand Family Literacy and Indigenous Storytelling
text:
Congratulations to the Joeten Kiyu Public Library who has been awarded a $200,000 grant from the Institute of Museum and Library Services through the Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian Program. The funding will support JKPL’s Families Reading Together: Planning a Sustainable Family Literacy and Indigenous Storytelling Initiative. This planning project will help develop family literacy programs that support parents in fostering their children’s reading development at home while incorporating Chamorro and Carolinian storytelling traditions. The project will assess community literacy needs, strengthen partnerships, adapt curriculum, and design pilot after-school family reading clubs. It will also explore the development of locally produced children’s books that reflect our islands’ culture and heritage. I congratulate JKPL, Ms. Erlinda Naputi, and the entire library team on this $200,000 federal award. This investment will help build a sustainable, culturally responsive family literacy program that strengthens family engagement with reading and benefits communities throughout the Northern Mariana Islands.

title: Building the CNMI’s Skilled Workforce
text: On Wednesday, I met with the Northern Marianas Technical Institute (NMTech) to discuss workforce and technical education priorities in the CNMI. We talked about CW-1 touchback challenges affecting ongoing disaster recovery projects and ways to strengthen our local skilled workforce. We also discussed NMTech’s campus development, federal accreditation efforts, and opportunities for veterans to use eligible education benefits. The importance of S.B. 24-47 was also brought to my attention. The bill is currently before the House Committee on Commerce and, if passed, would establish a CNMI contractor licensing system. S.B. 24-47 makes sense and complements federal efforts and resources aimed at supporting the training and advancement of U.S. workers in our labor force. If we want to grow our local workforce in the construction trades, raising industry standards and creating greater collaboration between the industry and the institutions training our workers is a great place to start. Thank you to the NMTech team for taking the time to sit down with me and for the work you continue doing to build opportunities for our people here at home.

title: Catching Up with Fabian Indalecio
text: Community advocate, health influencer, U.S.Military Veteran, and museum curator Fabian Indalecio stopped by the Saipan District Office last week to catch up on the work we are doing and some of the policies Congress is considering related to veterans benefits and what they could mean for veterans here in the CNMI. Fabian is a well-known face in our community, and it was a pleasure to hear from him, learn more about his passion for our islands, and connect on issues that matter to the people we serve. I always appreciate when members of our community take the time to stop by, ask questions, share their perspectives, and help us better understand the issues they care about. Thank you, Fabian!

title: Hill to the Vill Comes to Saipan and Tinian
text: Last week was jam-packed with... you! We held two of our town hall events that we call Hill to the Vill, and I am incredibly grateful to everyone who came out to join the conversation. These meetings with you are important to the work I am doing on your behalf. You should be able to hear directly from me. You should be able to ask questions about the work we're doing, why we're doing it, and share your ideas about where we should be working harder. Between our events on Tinian and Saipan, we covered a lot of ground. We talked about homelessness, disaster recovery, healthcare, deep-sea minerals, energy costs, global events, and much more. I sincerely appreciate everyone who came out in person or tuned in online and took the time to participate. If you missed either conversation, you can catch some of the coverage of our Tinian event here and our Saipan event here. And we're not done! We are working on the time and place for our Rota Hill to the Vill and look forward to bringing the conversation to our residents there. We'll share the details as soon as they're set, and I hope you'll come out, ask questions, share your thoughts, and be part of the work we're doing together.

title: Investing in Affordable and Reliable Power
text: On Monday, I introduced HR 10074, the Affordable Power for the Northern Marianas Act, legislation that would direct $15 million annually in existing Covenant funding back to the CNMI, with most of those resources dedicated to rebuilding our aging power system and helping reduce or stabilize electricity costs. Power costs affect nearly every part of life in the Commonwealth. They affect household budgets, the ability of businesses to grow and hire, the cost of operating our schools and hospital, and ultimately whether people can afford to build a future here at home. This bill would prioritize investments that lower fuel and operating costs, improve efficiency, and reduce the frequency and cost of outages. Importantly, the bill does not increase overall federal mandatory spending. It redirects a greater share of existing Covenant funding to the Commonwealth and removes local matching requirements for energy projects so that limited local resources do not prevent critical investments from moving forward. We have spent too long managing one power crisis after another. This legislation is about putting real resources behind a long-term solution and making affordable, reliable electricity a central part of rebuilding the CNMI economy.

title: Let’s Talk About it: Reporting Back on Our Progress
text: While I am home this August, I want to take some time to report back to you on the work we have been doing and the progress we have made over the last year and a half. In this week’s Let’s Talk About It, I take a step back from individual issues and walk through the bigger picture. That includes the bills we have introduced, CNMI provisions we have successfully moved through Congress and into law, millions of dollars in new federal resources we are working to bring home, and some of the major priorities we are still fighting to advance. There is much more work to do, and I want to move faster. But you deserve to know what we have accomplished, what is still moving through Congress, and where we are headed next. Take a few minutes to watch the video and hear directly from me about where things stand.

title: New Ruling Changes Advance Parole Travel Considerations
text: A recent decision by the Board of Immigration Appeals may have significant consequences for individuals with a history of unlawful presence who are considering travel outside the United States using advance parole. On August 13, the Board issued its decision in Matter of Delcarmen-Lara, overturning prior precedent that generally did not treat temporary travel under advance parole as a “departure” for purposes of the three-year and ten-year unlawful-presence bars. Under the new ruling, travel outside the United States using advance parole can now constitute a departure and may trigger these bars for individuals who have accrued the applicable period of unlawful presence. The Board stated that this new interpretation will apply prospectively. This is particularly important for individuals who have recently received advance parole, including emergency advance parole, and have not yet traveled. Having an approved advance parole document does not necessarily protect an individual from the immigration consequences that may result from departing the United States. If you believe this decision may apply to you, I strongly encourage you to speak with a qualified immigration attorney before traveling. Every immigration case is different, and individuals should understand how this new ruling may affect their particular status and circumstances before making travel plans.

title: The Patriot Games
text:
I’m proud to see two young athletes from the CNMI, Addalee Taflinger and Richard Zhao, representing our islands at the Patriot Games in Ohio. Addalee was recently featured in TIME, where she spoke about her desire to bring greater awareness to Saipan and the resilience of our people following devastating typhoons. I’m proud of both Addalee and Richard for representing the CNMI on this national stage and showing the country the talent, determination, and spirit of our young people. Congratulations to them both!

title: SBA Expands Bavi Disaster Assistance to Saipan and Tinian
text: The U.S. Small Business Administration has issued a rural disaster declaration for Saipan and Tinian following Super Typhoon Bavi, making additional federal disaster assistance available to eligible homeowners, renters, businesses, and nonprofit organizations on both islands. Rota is already covered through the Presidential disaster declaration for Bavi. The declaration makes several forms of assistance available, including loans of up to $500,000 for homeowners with real estate damage, up to $100,000 for personal property, and up to $2 million for businesses with physical damage. Economic Injury Disaster Loans are also available to eligible businesses and organizations that suffered economic losses because of the storm. The deadline to apply for physical damage assistance related to Bavi is October 13, 2026, while applications for economic injury assistance are due May 14, 2027. I want to thank the SBA for acting quickly on the Commonwealth's request and making these resources available to our community. If you experienced damage or economic impacts from Bavi, I encourage you to review the assistance available and apply. Even if you are uncertain whether you qualify, take the time to explore your options and make sure you are not leaving potential recovery assistance on the table.

title: Tracking Recovery and Securing Federal Support
text: I started the week with Governor Apatang and FEMA officials for an update on recovery and relief efforts following Super Typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi. I have been closely tracking the federal response and the progress of several major requests as we work to keep recovery moving across our islands. I was very happy to see President Trump authorize an extension of 100 percent federal coverage for debris removal, emergency protective measures, and Direct Federal Assistance associated with Super Typhoon Sinlaku. This means critical response and recovery work can continue without requiring the Commonwealth to immediately take on a share of these costs at a time when our local resources are already stretched. There is still a lot of work ahead for both Sinlaku and Bavi. During the meeting, I also continued pushing FEMA for the quick implementation of Disaster Unemployment Assistance so workers who lost income because of the storms can receive the support they need. I appreciate the opportunity to sit down together, get an update on where things stand, and continue advocating at the federal level to move our recovery forward.

title: Landsman, Hayes, Lofgren Lead Legislation to Invest in Quality Early Childhood Education
text:
Cincinnati, OH – Congressman Greg Landsman (D-OH-01), Congresswoman Jahanna Hayes (D-CT-05), and Congresswoman Zoe Lofgren (D-CA-18) introduced legislation to significantly invest in and improve the Head Start program.

Head Start is a federally funded program that provides free early childhood education and family support to help prepare children for school. Head Start is critical in our communities but is under-resourced, outdated, and understaffed.

In response, Reps. Landsman, Hayes, and Lofgren introduced the Head Start Expansion and Improvement Act – comprehensive legislation to triple annual funding for Head Start and Early Head Start to $36 billion for Fiscal Years 2027-2032.

The Head Start Expansion and Improvement Act would:

Expand eligibility to include families who are at or below 138 percent of the Federal Poverty Level.

Expand eligibility to include families who are eligible for TANF, SSI, SNAP, WIC, or CHIP.

Establish a grant program to renovate, expand, and acquire facilities.

Establish a grant program to increase salaries for Head Start and Early Head Start workers.

Provide student loan forgiveness for Head Start and Early Head Start workers.

Congressman Landsman:

“High quality preschool makes such a difference in our children’s lives, and Head Start gives families the support they need to succeed. Our legislation will help more families give their children the best possible start.”

Congresswoman Hayes:

“Head Start is one of the greatest anti-poverty programs that we have. It offers high-quality education, health, and social services to the youngest and most vulnerable among us during a critical developmental stage. The Head Start Expansion and Improvement Act demands immediate action in addressing the growing needs of this vital program and allows more families to access its services.”

Congresswoman Lofgren:

“It’s critical that America’s children receive a first-class education and have opportunities that create a solid learning foundation. Under the Trump administration, critical federal education programs and agencies have been increasingly under threat. For more than 60 years, Head Start has played an important role in helping children enter school ready to learn and succeed. I am proud to join Reps. Hayes and Landsman in introducing the Head Start Expansion and Improvement Act to protect and preserve the Head Start program.”
